name: Sexually Transmitted Infections: Overview and Clinical Approach

clinicalPearls: STIs are syndrome-driven in practice: most patients are managed initially by presenting symptoms, signs, and risk factors rather than by a confirmed microbial diagnosis, with common syndromes including male urethritis, epididymitis, mucopurulent cervicitis, vulvovaginitis, genital/perianal ulcers, PID, and proctitis (Harrison 22e p.1100).

More than 40 microorganisms are now recognized as predominantly sexually transmitted or frequently sexually transmissible, spanning bacteria, viruses, protozoa, fungi, and ectoparasites (Harrison 22e p.1096).

The initial rate of spread of any STI in a population is the product of three factors: the rate of sexual exposure of susceptible to infectious persons, the per-exposure transmission efficiency, and the duration of infectivity (Harrison 22e p.1096).

Genital HPV is described as the most common sexually transmitted pathogen in the United States, and HPV and hepatitis B virus remain major causes of cervical and hepatocellular carcinoma respectively in the developing world (Harrison 22e p.1096-1097).

Reported syphilis in the United States in 2022 (207,255 cases, all stages and congenital) was the highest since 1950, with congenital syphilis rate of 102.5 per 100,000 live births and 282 congenital syphilis-related stillbirths/infant deaths (Harrison 22e p.1097).

All four major curable STIs (gonorrhea, chlamydial infection, syphilis, trichomoniasis) plus bacterial vaginosis have been associated with increased risk of HIV transmission or acquisition (Harrison 22e p.1097).

Acute epididymitis in sexually active men under 35 is most often due to C. trachomatis (less often N. gonorrhoeae) and usually accompanies overt or subclinical urethritis, whereas in older men or after urinary instrumentation it is usually caused by urinary pathogens (Harrison 22e p.1101).

Unsolicited reporting of abnormal vaginal discharge (increased amount or abnormal odor) most often denotes bacterial vaginosis or trichomoniasis, not cervical gonorrhea or chlamydia, which usually do not increase discharge volume or odor (Harrison 22e p.1101).

Sexually transmitted HSV causes most genital ulcer disease worldwide; HSV-2 produces more frequent genital recurrences and is more infectious to partners than HSV-1, so typing has prognostic value (Harrison 22e p.1097, 1108).

STI control combines reducing exposure (education, behavior change, post-exposure prophylaxis), shortening infectivity (early diagnosis and curative or suppressive treatment), and reducing per-exposure transmission (condoms, vaccines, male medical circumcision) (Harrison 22e p.1096).
Despite the strong epidemiologic HSV-HIV link, randomized trials of antiviral HSV suppression showed no protective effect against HIV acquisition or transmission (Harrison 22e p.1097).
harrison.pathophysiology: STIs are acquired through sexual exposure to a susceptible person from an infectious one, with spread amplified within highly interconnected sexual networks marked by high partner-change rates or concurrent partners (e.g., transactional sex, some MSM, drug-using populations), while infections such as chlamydia, genital HPV, and genital herpes propagate efficiently even in relatively low-risk populations. Many of these organisms colonize or invade genital, anal, oral, or systemic epithelium; ascending spread from cervix or vagina to endometrium and fallopian tubes underlies PID, with potential extension to pelvic peritonitis, perihepatitis, perisplenitis, or abscess. Immunopathology contributes to tissue damage in chlamydial salpingitis, where repeated exposure produces the greatest inflammation. Hormonal and anatomic factors modulate susceptibility (e.g., cervical ectopy may increase susceptibility to gonococcus, chlamydia, and HIV; oral contraceptives favor ectopy persistence; menstruation appears to facilitate ascending gonococcal/chlamydial infection).
additionalDifferentials: Acute epididymitis must be distinguished from testicular torsion (a surgical emergency with sudden pain, testicular elevation, and absent Doppler flow), testicular tumor, and trauma (Harrison 22e p.1101)

Dysuric women: STI-associated urethral syndrome (sterile pyuria, <10^2 conventional uropathogens/mL) versus bacterial cystitis (single uropathogen >=10^2/mL) versus acute pyelonephritis (costovertebral tenderness/fever) (Harrison 22e p.1100-1101)
Persistent genital ulcer not resolving with syndrome-based therapy: consider donovanosis, carcinoma, and other nonvenereal dermatoses on biopsy (Harrison 22e p.1108)
infectionMimics: Pelvic inflammatory disease that is not due to specific STIs (secondary to appendicitis, regional ileitis, diverticulitis, hematogenous tuberculosis or staphylococcal bacteremia, or tropical disease such as schistosomiasis) (Harrison 22e p.1104)
Chronic granulomatous epididymal disease such as tuberculosis mimicking sexually acquired epididymitis when symptoms persist after therapy (Harrison 22e p.1101)
nonInfectiousMimics: Cervical ectopy (columnar epithelium on the ectocervix), often mislabeled 'cervical erosion,' confused with infectious endocervicitis but showing clear/cloudy mucus and intact epithelium on colposcopy (Harrison 22e p.1104)
Testicular tumor or trauma presenting as scrotal pain/swelling mimicking epididymitis (Harrison 22e p.1101)
Genital carcinoma or nonvenereal dermatoses presenting as a persistent genital ulcer (Harrison 22e p.1108)
additionalInvestigations: Risk assessment using a structured sexual-history questionnaire (e.g., the eleven-question STD/HIV risk assessment) to guide screening and presumptive treatment decisions (Harrison 22e p.1098)
Urethral Gram's stain to confirm urethritis and detect gram-negative diplococci, recognizing that up to ~30% of gonococcal urethral infections can yield a negative Gram's stain (Harrison 22e p.1099)
Nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) for N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis, M. genitalium, and T. vaginalis on appropriate genital/urine specimens (Harrison 22e p.1099-1100)

Genital ulcer workup: dark-field examination, direct fluorescent antibody, or PCR for T. pallidum; RPR/VDRL/EIA serology for syphilis; culture, FA, ELISA, or PCR for HSV; HSV-2 type-specific serology; PCR or culture for H. ducreyi in chancroid-endemic settings (Harrison 22e p.1108-1109)
Biopsy of a genital ulcer persisting beyond the expected natural history (herpes 2-3 weeks; chancroid or syphilis up to 6 weeks) to exclude donovanosis and malignancy (Harrison 22e p.1108)
Aspiration of fluctuant inguinal nodes for culture/PCR (H. ducreyi) plus Gram's stain to exclude other pyogenic bacteria (Harrison 22e p.1108)
redFlags: Sudden severe testicular pain with testicular elevation and absent Doppler flow indicating testicular torsion, a surgical emergency (Harrison 22e p.1101)
Costovertebral angle pain/tenderness or fever in a dysuric woman suggesting acute pyelonephritis (Harrison 22e p.1100)
Genital ulcer in a patient with HIV risk (e.g., MSM, known HIV infection): treat presumptively for syphilis rather than awaiting seroconversion given high syphilis rates (Harrison 22e p.1108)
Suspected PID with peritoneal extension (pelvic or generalized peritonitis, perihepatitis, perisplenitis, or pelvic abscess) (Harrison 22e p.1104)
Congenital syphilis exposure in pregnancy, given the sharp recent rise including syphilis-related stillbirths and infant deaths (Harrison 22e p.1097)
harrison.prognosis: Many STIs are curable when diagnosed and treated early, and prompt treatment shortens infectivity and reduces onward transmission. Outcomes worsen with delayed care: untreated chlamydial and gonococcal infection can ascend to cause PID with risk of tubal damage and infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and chronic pelvic pain, and immunopathology contributes to chlamydial tubal injury. HPV and HBV carry long-term oncogenic risk (cervical and other anogenital cancers; hepatocellular carcinoma). HSV-2 causes lifelong recurrent infection with asymptomatic shedding and ongoing transmission risk. In men, urethritis with neither chlamydiae nor gonococci detected carries a higher risk of recurrent nongonococcal urethritis, and most persistent urethritis is attributable to M. genitalium. Congenital syphilis can result in stillbirth or infant death.
pitfalls: Treating genital symptoms without performing the microbiologic tests needed to establish a cause; self-diagnosis of vulvovaginal candidiasis is often incorrect (Harrison 22e p.1101)
Relying on urethral Gram's stain alone to exclude gonorrhea, since up to ~30% of gonococcal urethral infections are smear-negative (Harrison 22e p.1099)
Misreading cervical ectopy as infectious endocervicitis and unnecessarily cauterizing it (Harrison 22e p.1104)

Assuming a positive HSV-2 serology proves current lesions are herpetic, when nearly one-fifth of the U.S. population becomes HSV-2 seropositive in early adulthood and type-specific assays are not 100% specific (Harrison 22e p.1108)
Failing to evaluate and treat sexual partners with contact in the relevant window (e.g., within the prior 60 days for urethritis), allowing reinfection (Harrison 22e p.1099)
Withholding presumptive syphilis treatment in a high-risk patient with a genital ulcer while awaiting seroconversion (Harrison 22e p.1108)

Attributing male urethritis recurrence to treatment failure without considering reexposure to an untreated partner or M. genitalium (often resistant to doxycycline and azithromycin) (Harrison 22e p.1100, 1099)
harrison.severityClassification: No single staging system applies to STIs as a group; severity is assessed by syndrome and complications. Localized lower-tract syndromes (uncomplicated urethritis, cervicitis, vulvovaginitis, genital ulcer) are distinguished from complicated or upper-tract/disseminated disease (PID with peritonitis, perihepatitis, perisplenitis, or pelvic abscess; disseminated gonococcal infection; epididymo-orchitis), and from long-term oncologic or reproductive sequelae (cervical/anogenital neoplasia, infertility). Genital ulcer evaluation also uses lesion natural-history timelines (herpes 2-3 weeks; chancroid and syphilis up to ~6 weeks) to flag atypical persistence (Harrison 22e p.1104, 1108).
management: Syndromic management with empirical treatment directed at the likely pathogens for the presenting syndrome (urethritis, cervicitis, genital ulcer, pelvic inflammatory disease, proctitis) pending confirmatory testing

Pathogen-directed antimicrobials once confirmed: ceftriaxone plus doxycycline for gonococcal and chlamydial infection, benzathine penicillin for syphilis, aciclovir-class antivirals for herpes, and nitroimidazoles for trichomoniasis
Partner notification, testing, and treatment (including expedited partner therapy where permitted) to interrupt transmission
Test for co-infections including HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B, and offer HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis to those at risk
Prevention through condom promotion, HPV and hepatitis B vaccination, and risk-reduction counselling
Follow-up with test-of-cure where indicated and abstinence until treatment is completed
Escalate pelvic inflammatory disease or systemic or complicated infection for inpatient parenteral therapy and genitourinary medicine input
